questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main mechanism for explaining the post-dot-com startup culture?
choices: A crash created an overcorrection that turned caution into doctrine
A crash proved that ambition is usually irrational
A crash showed that only product quality matters in startups

explanation.gentle: The chapter does not say the crash taught nothing. It says the lessons became too broad and too permanent.
explanation.direct: Overcorrection is the key concept. A real warning hardened into universal startup philosophy.
explanation.competitive: The chapter's point is not anti-ambition. It is anti-fear masquerading as timeless wisdom.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs to the safer rulebook the chapter criticizes?
choices: Focus on product, not sales
Pursue monopoly before product-market fit
Ignore competition because all markets are empty

explanation.gentle: The chapter names four post-crash rules, and this is one of them.
explanation.direct: Product-not-sales is part of the inherited rulebook the chapter treats as only partially true.
explanation.competitive: That line sounds pure, which is exactly why it became such a comfortable hiding place.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat the four lessons as more dangerous than obvious nonsense?
choices: Because they are too technical for founders to understand correctly
Because each contains partial truth and therefore spreads easily as universal advice
Because they were invented long after the crash by business schools

explanation.gentle: Partial truths travel far because they sound reasonable in many situations, even when they no longer fit well.
explanation.direct: The chapter's criticism is about universality. A context-sensitive safeguard becomes weak when treated as permanent law.
explanation.competitive: Bad doctrine survives best when it contains just enough truth to avoid suspicion.

questions.prompt: Mara proposes a sharper one-year plan, and her cofounder calls commitment itself reckless. Which chapter lesson fits best?
choices: Commitment is usually less serious than flexibility after any market crash
The culture may be rewarding defendability over a strategically necessary wager
The company should focus on product and ignore planning for now

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that flexibility can become a status signal instead of a tool.
explanation.direct: This is overcorrection in action: commitment looks suspect before its strategic value is even tested.
explanation.competitive: Fear is winning the room early by making vagueness sound mature.

questions.prompt: A student team prefers a safer incremental project because everyone agrees it sounds sensible after studying startup crashes. What would the chapter ask first?
choices: Does the safe project actually create a stronger company shape, or is it just easier to defend?
How can the team remove every possible risk before deciding?
How can the team avoid looking contrarian to professors and mentors?

explanation.gentle: The chapter asks whether caution is serving judgment or simply lowering the chance of embarrassment.
explanation.direct: This is the overcorrection test: strategic strength versus social legibility.
explanation.competitive: If the project wins because it feels harder to criticize, that is not the same as winning because it is stronger.

questions.prompt: Theo says he wants to stay focused on product and not get distracted by sales talk. What is the chapter's strongest concern?
choices: He is proving the product must already be strong enough to spread on its own
He may be using product purity to hide a distribution weakness
He is correctly treating sales as morally inferior to engineering

explanation.gentle: The chapter's criticism is narrow but clear: avoiding sales language does not solve the commercial problem.
explanation.direct: Product quality matters, but anti-sales posture can become a cover for distribution blindness.
explanation.competitive: Theo may sound principled while simply ducking the harder half of company building.

questions.prompt: Why does improving on the competition become a weak universal rule in this chapter?
choices: Because competitors are always irrelevant once a company launches
Because it can keep founders trapped inside categories defined by other firms
Because the chapter thinks all competition should be ignored emotionally

explanation.gentle: The chapter worries that competitor-focused thinking can narrow imagination before strategy begins.
explanation.direct: Improvement inside an existing frame may still leave the frame itself unchallenged.
explanation.competitive: If rivals define the game, you can get better at losing their game instead of building your own.

questions.prompt: June discovers that her modest plan feels rational partly because it lowers the chance she will look naive if she fails. What does the chapter suggest?
choices: Her smaller plan is therefore objectively stronger
She should always ignore social embarrassment because only data matters
She may be mixing strategic caution with reputation protection

explanation.gentle: The chapter says fear can survive inside smart-sounding rules, so the emotional motive needs to be named.
explanation.direct: This is a key distinction: judgment and ego protection can overlap, but they should not be treated as identical.
explanation.competitive: If June cannot separate risk from shame-avoidance, fear keeps writing her strategy.

questions.prompt: Why is overcorrection more damaging than a single bad rule in this chapter's logic?
choices: Because it reshapes what kinds of companies seem respectable before specific strategy questions are even asked
Because it makes founders incapable of learning anything from failure ever again
Because it eliminates all useful differences between industries

explanation.gentle: The chapter cares about culture because culture changes what even feels reasonable to attempt.
explanation.direct: Overcorrection sets an ambition ceiling at the level of common sense, which is broader than any one tactical mistake.
explanation.competitive: Once fear becomes doctrine, it stops guiding choices and starts shrinking the field of choices.

questions.prompt: If Chapter 1 argued for definite creation, what does Chapter 2 add before the book moves on?
choices: It shows why a crash-era culture may punish the very conviction definite creation requires
It proves that every cautious rule after failure should be discarded immediately
It replaces planning with pure improvisation as the best startup method

explanation.gentle: The chapter connects the book's opening idea to the cultural fear that makes that idea harder to live out.
explanation.direct: Chapter 2 explains why definite creation became psychologically and culturally suspect after the crash.
explanation.competitive: It shows why builders can agree with boldness in theory while still obeying fear in practice.
